ordeals.excerpt: They even passed scatheless through the first ordeal of the House of Gloom. The Xibalbans were furious, and their wrath was by no means allayed when they found themselves beaten at the game of ball to which they had challenged the brothers. Then Hun-Came and Vukub-Came ordered the twins to bring them four bouquets of flowers, asking the guards of the royal gardens to watch most carefully, and committed Hun-Ahpu and Xbalanque to the "House of Lances"--the second ordeal--where the lancers were directed to kill them. The brothers, however, had at their beck and call a swarm of ants, which entered the royal gardens on the first errand, and they succeeded in bribing the lancers. The Xibalbans, white with fury, ordered that the owls, the guardians of the gardens, should have their lips split, and otherwise showed their anger at their third defeat. Then came the third ordeal in the "House of Cold." Here the heroes escaped death by freezing by being warmed with burning pine-cones. In the fourth and fifth ordeals they were equally lucky, for they passed a night each in the "House of Tigers" and the "House of Fire" without injury. But at the sixth ordeal misfortune overtook them in the "House of Bats." Hun-Ahpu's head being cut off by Camazotz, "Ruler of Bats," who suddenly appeared from above.
ordeals.note: Verbatim prose from Spence's 1908 English summary, which he says draws on Brasseur de Bourbourg's French and Ximénez's Spanish translations. This is not a direct translation of the K'iche' text.

narrativeBlocks.title: The first test is a trap
narrativeBlocks.body: Spence describes the twins avoiding the red-hot seat and passing the House of Gloom before the rulers set further ordeals.

narrativeBlocks.title: A series of dangerous houses

narrativeBlocks.title: The House of Bats is different
narrativeBlocks.body: The twins survive the Houses of Cold, Tigers, and Fire, but in the House of Bats Hun-Ahpu is beheaded by Camazotz.

narrativeBlocks.title: The summary admits uncertainty
narrativeBlocks.body: Spence says the account does not make clear how Hun-Ahpu recovers from the wound, because the text is unintelligible at that point. Do not fill that gap with invented certainty.

narrativeBlocks.title: Survival does not erase the textual gap
narrativeBlocks.body: The episode names several ordeals and records a severe injury, while Spence explicitly marks the recovery sequence as unclear.
